title: Praise and blame
hook: if others praise or blame the Buddha, the monks should be neither elated nor angry

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Digha Nikaya, and your line, the long ones. Did one conversation run longer than usual? Today the long collection begins, on a dusty road. Day five hundred twenty-three.

The first long discourse starts on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda. The Buddha is walking with a large group of monks. Behind them, on the same road, come two more travelers: a wandering teacher named Suppiya and his young student Brahmadatta. And all the way, they're arguing. Suppiya is running down the Buddha, his teaching and his monks. His own student is praising all three. Teacher and pupil, walking right behind, saying opposite things. That night everyone stops at the same rest house. Today: praise and blame.
screen: `THE ROAD TO NALANDA.` → `ONE BLAMES, ONE PRAISES.` → `THE SAME REST HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Next morning, the monks are talking it over. Amazing, isn't it, the two of them, one praising and one blaming, all the way down the road. The Buddha walks in and asks what they're discussing. Then he gives the instruction that opens the whole long collection. If others speak against me, he says, or against the teaching, or against the community, don't be angry or resentful or upset. Why not? First, because it would be an obstacle for you. And second, because if you were angry, could you even tell whether what they said was true or false? The monks admit they couldn't. So instead, he says, if something said is false, calmly explain that it's false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us. And then the other half, which is easier to miss. If others speak in praise of me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be elated or delighted or puffed up. That too would be an obstacle. If what they say is true, simply acknowledge it: yes, that's so, that's found among us. The Pali words are vanna and avanna: praise and dispraise. Notice the symmetry. Praise is treated as just as risky as blame. Both cloud the mind, and a clouded mind can't check facts. The instruction isn't to stop caring what's true. It's the opposite. Stay level, so you can see what's true. And the monks are told to do it for their own teacher, not just for themselves. Even loyalty is supposed to stay calm.
screen: `THE MONKS TALK IT OVER` · `BLAME: DON'T BE ANGRY` · `PRAISE: DON'T BE ELATED` · `STAY LEVEL TO SEE WHAT'S TRUE` · then, large: `NOT ELATED, NOT ANGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay level at praise. Remember a compliment you got recently. Let it play back. Notice the lift in the chest, the warm glow. Don't push it away. Just ask: is it true? Part of it? All of it? Now remember a criticism, a small one. Notice the drop, the heat. Ask the same question: is it true? Part? Let both sit side by side, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Vanna. Praise (its opposite is avanna, dispraise): neither to be angry at nor elated by, so the mind stays clear enough to tell what's true. Today's word.
Your line: not elated, not angry. Today, when praise or blame comes your way, pause and ask only: what here is true? Day five hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across schools speak of the eight worldly winds (gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain), and practitioners train to meet them with equanimity, as the opening of DN 1 describes.

match.prompt: praise and blame: tap the pairs.
pairs: don't be angry; explain what's false
don't be elated; acknowledge what's true

myth: the Buddha tells his monks to defend him hotly against critics
he says anger would be an obstacle, and they couldn't even tell what was true.
praise is treated as a risk too
being elated is also an obstacle, so the monks are told not to be puffed up.
the critic and the admirer in the story are teacher and student
Suppiya blames, and his own student Brahmadatta praises.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks. someone on the road says false things about your teacher. what does DN 1 say to do?
options: stay calm and explain that it isn't so.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says don't be angry, it would cloud you; calmly explain what's false as false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us.

original.note: Pali vanna: praise (also color, appearance); avanna: dispraise. the two winds the monks must meet calmly.

trapdoor: what you thought: praise is good and blame is bad.
what it means: in DN 1 both are risks, because elation and anger both cloud the mind.
what a scholar hears: this frame story opens the Brahmajala Sutta and leads straight into the long passage on morality, which shows that what outsiders usually praise is the least of the teaching.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (the supreme net), opening section

notes: DN 1 paraphrased. Rhys Davids' 1899 translation is public domain, but its exact wording was not reproduced; a Keeper may wish to add a short exact quotation.
